latin.324: Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis, adhuc in utero matrum delitescentes aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragat. Videras hanc rationem, cur ei non acquievisti? Non satisfit, inquis, si quis dicat esse peccatores, quia peccato inquinatos, esse mortales. Id quidem verum est, sed necessario admittendum est, eos nullum habere peccatum, nisi illud originale, quod non est peccatum ipsorum, nisi quatenus sunt filii Adami; & quatenus ab ipso orti & procreati, in ipso peccaverunt, & inobedientia & culpa illius ipsis imputatur. Aut te non intelligo, aut hic incipis quod sentis aperire, nullum esse peccatum originale praeter illud actuale Adami nobis imputatum.
latin.325: Quae Pighii & Catharini, & Salmeronis fuit sententia ab Ecclesiis nostris iure damnata: nam si credis in infantibus vitium esse originale inhaerens, quod vere peccatum sit, quod generi humano damnando sufficiat, quod infantes in utero materno delitescentes aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragat, cur tibi quaerenti, cur infantes moriantur, non satisfacit qui respondet, in illis causam esse mortis vitium seu peccatum hereditario inhaerens? Hoc enim est mortis infantium proximam causam afferre, cuius remota est lapsus Adami.
latin.326: Si rursus quaeras, cur hoc vitium puerulis insit, Respondebo cum Iobo, ex immundo fieri mundum non posse, Et cum ipso Christo, quod ex carne natum est, carnem esse. Quam homo hominem, tam immundus immundum, corruptus corruptum genuit, secundum leges naturae. Quid est quamobrem haec responsio tibi non satisfaciat? an quia non capis quomodo vitium propagari possit & a parente in prolis animam transfundi? atqui nihil in ea re est difficultatis, praeter eam quae oritur ex creatione animae rationalis: quam difficultatem thesibus meis tollere conatus sum ea ratione, quam tu, quia non intellexisti, carpis quidem in extremo tui tractatus Capite, sed nullo modo refutas. Frustra enim laboratur in refutando id, quod non intelligitur. Ad eum locum cum pervenero, Deo bene iuvante, meipsum explicabo. An quia non capis, quomodo unum actuale peccatum invehere potuerit in Adamum corruptionem moralem una cum natura propagandam? Atqui huius rei rationem in thesibus reddideram, quam a te rejectam aut reprehensam in toto isto tuo tractatu non legi.
latin.327: Vis dicam ingenue quid intersit inter tuam sententiam & meam? Ego eo tendo, ut omnium malorum generis humani fons & causa in ipsum genus humanum, non autem in Deum referatur. Tua vero sententia eo spectat, ut ipsi Deo attribuatur: quod ego, qua erga Creatorem & Redemptorem meum ducor reverentia, pati non possum. Vitium inhaerens fons est omnium peccatorum actualium. Constat inter nos id ducere originem a primo peccato actuali Adami. Sed quaeritur primo, quae sit ratio, cur primum peccatum actuale Adamum corruperit? Ego id ascribo ipsi illius primi peccati naturae, quod fuit mutatio summi boni, seu finis ultimi, hoc est, apostasia a Deo, tanquam invido & malevolo, & conversio ad creaturas tanquam ad summum bonum, seu finem ultimum, contra Dei verbum. Quoniam autem quicquid appetimus est, aut finis, aut medium ad finem, & media omnia, omnesque fines subordinatos finis ultimus continet sibi colligatos, eo mutato secuta est universalis mutatio eorum omnium, quae in Adamo moralia fuerunt, quam mutationem subsecuta mala conscientia Deum refugiens & horrens, ut offensum, ut iratum, ut iudicem, ut hostem, auxit & confirmavit. Tu vero non dubitas id, quicquid est, ipsi Deo adscribere, qui iustitiam subtraxerit Adamo, eumque privaverit rectitudine & sanctitate, ut sic puniret peccatum actuale, & iustitiae suae satisfaceret.
latin.328: Quaeritur secundo, cur peccato corruptus ac vitiatus Adamus filios genuerit similiter corruptos? Ego corruptionis illius naturae id tribuo, quae universalis cum esset, ipsam vim generatricem, quatenus moralis quaedam facultas est, corrupit, & infecit, & convertit ad generationem, non ut ad medium, sed ut ad finem ultimum. Porro finis ultimus, cum ab alio non definiatur, aut pendeat, sed ab eo omnia, natura sua infinitus est. Itaque in eum feruntur facultates sine limitatione, aut modo, quodammodo infinite. Postquam igitur in locum veri finis ultimi, hoc est, Dei successit falso apparens, fallax nempe felicitatis species reperiendae in creaturis, immoderate, absque freno, absque limitatione, corrupte, depravateque circa generationem versata est, tanquam circa finem ultimum facultas generandi, parte animae superiore, eodem conversa una cum appetitu sensitivo, non cohibente, sed impellente.
latin.329: A facultate sic corrupta ac depravate agente elaboratum est semen corruptum, hoc est, consentaneum ac congruens cum depravata facultati generatrici, tum etiam aliis facultatibus quas generatrix semine adumbrare & exprimere quam accuratissime conatur. Quomodo autem haec vitiositas a semine ad animam rationalem transeat; suo loco, hoc est, ad Cap. ultimum tractatus tui Deo dante exponam. GAR. Primum id ab eo quaerimus, quod ipse a nobis alibi, Unde id habes? Ex Scripturisne, an aliunde? aut quomodo demonstras, hoc non esse inter figmenta habendum, quae inani subtilitatis umbra curiosulos delectant? PLAC. Quaesivi unde haberetis, qui cum disputabam, quod dicebat de interno quodam mentis & voluntatis divinae actu, non aliunde quam ex revelatione divina noscendo. Hic vero quid dixi eiusmodi, quod non vel Scriptura, vel ratione, vel experientia ipsa firmari possit?

pass_a.324: The Confession Art. XI: this inherent vice is truly sin and makes every human—infants still in the womb not excepted—guilty of eternal death before God. Placeus asks why GAR would not rest there. GAR: saying they are sinners because stained, and so mortal, is not enough; one must admit they have no sin but original, theirs only as Adam's sons who sinned in him, his disobedience imputed. Placeus: either I miss you, or you are opening that there is no original sin besides Adam's actual sin imputed to us.
pass_a.325: That is Pighius, Catharinus, and Salmeron's view, rightly damned by our Churches. If you grant infants an inherent original vice that is truly sin, enough to damn the race and make womb-hidden infants guilty of eternal death, why does 'hereditarily inherent vice is their death-cause' not answer why they die? That names the proximate cause; Adam's fall is the remote.
pass_a.326: Why the vice in little ones? Job: unclean cannot make clean; Christ: born of flesh is flesh. As man begets man, unclean begets unclean under nature's laws. If the stick is how vice pours into the offspring's soul, the only hard bit is rational-soul creation—which Placeus tried to ease in his theses, and which GAR carps at without understanding or refuting. Vain labor to refute what is not understood; Placeus will explain at that place, God helping. Or if the stick is how one actual sin lodged moral corruption to propagate with nature, that reason was already in the theses and Placeus has not seen it answered in this whole treatise.
pass_a.327: Frankly Placeus aims to seat the fountain and cause of all the human race's evils in the human race itself, not in God; GAR's line tends to charge God Himself—which reverence for Creator and Redeemer forbids Placeus to endure. Inherent vice is the fountain of all actual sins, and both agree it draws from Adam's first actual sin. Why did that first act corrupt Adam? Placeus ascribes it to the sin's own nature as change of highest good or last end—apostasy from God as envious and malevolent, turning to creatures as highest good against God's word. Since whatever we desire is end or means, and the last end binds all means and subordinate ends, when the last end changed there followed a universal change of all that was moral in Adam, worsened by a bad conscience fleeing God as offended judge and enemy. GAR ascribes the same stripping of righteousness and holiness to God punishing actual sin and satisfying justice.
pass_a.328: Second question: why did Adam, corrupted by sin, beget sons similarly corrupted? Placeus attributes that to the nature of the corruption which, being universal, corrupted and infected the generative force itself insofar as it is a moral faculty, turning generation from a means into a last end. A last end is unlimited by nature—faculties run at it without bridle. Once a false creaturely happiness replaced God as last end, the generative faculty worked generation immoderately and corruptly as if last end, superior soul and sensitive appetite driving rather than restraining.
pass_a.329: From that depraved faculty came corrupt seed congruent with it and with the other powers the generative tries to imprint in the seed. How viciousness passes from seed to rational soul Placeus defers to GAR's last chapter, God granting. GAR presses what Placeus had pressed elsewhere: whence—Scripture or elsewhere—or is this curious fiction under a shade of subtlety? Placeus answers that he demanded revelation for GAR's internal divine act; here he claims nothing that Scripture, reason, or experience itself cannot firm. Tip before the moral-generative faculty quarrel.

324: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes all and each of men—little ones not excepted, even while still hiding in their mothers' womb—guilty of eternal death before God. You had seen this reason: why did you not rest in it? It does not satisfy, you say, if someone says they are sinners because stained with sin, and so mortal. That is indeed true, but it must necessarily be admitted that they have no sin except that original, which is not their own sin except insofar as they are sons of Adam; and insofar as sprung and begotten from him, they sinned in him, and his disobedience and guilt is imputed to them. Either I do not understand you, or here you begin to open what you think: that there is no original sin besides that actual sin of Adam imputed to us.
325: Which was the opinion of Pighius and Catharinus and Salmeron, rightly condemned by our Churches: for if you believe there is in infants an original inherent vice which is truly sin, which suffices for damning the human race, which makes infants hiding in the maternal womb guilty of eternal death before God—why, when you ask why infants die, does it not satisfy the one who answers that in them the cause of death is the vice or sin hereditarily inherent? For this is to give the proximate cause of infants' death, whose remote cause is Adam's fall.
326: If again you ask why this vice is in little children, I will answer with Job, that from the unclean a clean cannot be made, and with Christ Himself, that what is born of flesh is flesh. As man begot man, so the unclean begot the unclean, the corrupt the corrupt, according to nature's laws. Why then does this answer not satisfy you? Is it because you do not grasp how vice can be propagated and poured from parent into the offspring's soul? Yet there is no difficulty in that matter beyond what arises from the creation of the rational soul—which difficulty I tried to remove in my theses by a reason which you, because you did not understand it, carp at in the last chapter of your treatise, but in no way refute. For it is vain labor to refute what is not understood. When I come to that place, God helping, I will explain myself. Or is it because you do not grasp how one actual sin could bring into Adam a moral corruption to be propagated with the nature? Yet I had given the reason of this in the theses, which I have not read rejected or blamed by you in this whole treatise of yours.
327: Shall I say frankly what differs between your opinion and mine? I aim that the fountain and cause of all the human race's evils be referred to the human race itself, not to God. But your opinion looks to attributing it to God Himself: which I, by the reverence I bear toward my Creator and Redeemer, cannot endure. Inherent vice is the fountain of all actual sins. It is agreed between us that it draws origin from Adam's first actual sin. But it is asked first: what is the reason why that first actual sin corrupted Adam? I ascribe it to the very nature of that first sin, which was a change of the highest good, or last end—that is, apostasy from God as envious and malevolent, and turning to creatures as to the highest good or last end, against God's word. And since whatever we desire is either an end or a means to an end, and the last end contains bound to itself all means and all subordinate ends, when it was changed there followed a universal change of all that was moral in Adam; which change a bad conscience fleeing and dreading God—as offended, as angry, as judge, as enemy—increased and confirmed. But you do not hesitate to ascribe whatever it is to God Himself, who withdrew righteousness from Adam and deprived him of uprightness and holiness, so as thus to punish the actual sin and satisfy His justice.
328: It is asked second: why did Adam, corrupted and vitiated by sin, beget sons similarly corrupted? I attribute that to the nature of that corruption which, being universal, corrupted and infected the generative force itself, insofar as it is a certain moral faculty, and turned it to generation not as to a means but as to a last end. Further, the last end, since it is not defined or dependent on another but all things on it, is infinite by its nature. And so the faculties are carried toward it without limitation or measure, in a way infinitely. After therefore in place of the true last end, that is God, there succeeded a falsely appearing, deceitful appearance of happiness to be found in creatures, the generative faculty dealt with generation immoderately, without bridle, without limitation, corruptly and depravedly, as around a last end—the superior part of the soul turned the same way together with the sensitive appetite, not restraining but driving.
329: From a faculty so corrupted and acting depravedly a corrupt seed was wrought—that is, agreeable and congruent with the depraved generative faculty, and also with the other faculties which the generative power tries as accurately as possible to sketch and express in the seed. But how this viciousness passes from seed to the rational soul I will explain, God granting, in its place—that is, at the last chapter of your treatise. GAR. First we ask of him what he elsewhere asked of us: Whence do you have that? From the Scriptures, or from elsewhere? Or how do you show this is not to be counted among fictions which delight the curious with an empty shade of subtlety? PLAC. I asked whence you had it, when I was disputing, of what he said about a certain internal act of the divine mind and will, to be known from nowhere but divine revelation. But here what have I said of that sort which cannot be firmed by Scripture, or by reason, or by experience itself?
